records.author: willlzl
records.storyText:
When agent ships code faster and faster, human review is no longer possible. Which brings 2 problems, at least for me:

1. I need to understand what my agent changes as quickly and easily as possible, cuz I don't wanna lose track of the current status of my product, or be the main bottleneck in shipping code.

2. I don't trust what my agent tells me. Many times, I've been suffered from agent telling me "all is well", then say "you are right, sorry, I missed..." after code failed on production.

To mitigate those problems, I made Genesis, a skill for coding agent to generate a beautiful flow chart to understand all the business flows, flag all risk changes and untested code between commits. It worked very well on me, so I benchmarked it against vanilla Claude code and Codex:

Vanilla → With Genesis 1. Test gaps caught: Claude Code 8% → 38% · Codex 4% → 23%

2. False alarms per review: Claude Code 2.1 → 0.7 · Codex 1.4 → 0.5

records.author: nadis
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Nadia, one of the makers of CadYam. My cofounder Jared is here to answer questions as well.

CadYam is a desktop design app built for a person and an AI agent to work on the same project: a CAD drawing, a video, an interior design plan, a data analysis, etc. You can sketch something by asking it to your agent and drop a pin on a specific place to ask for changes.

We built this after a lot of frustration trying to learn traditional CAD tools, which have a steep learning curve and take a lot of time and effort before you can build anything complex. With CadYam, the agent can do the work for you with your guidance or teach you how to use the app if you'd like to do some manual work yourself, so you also don't always need the agent.

The agent's changes show up as a preview you iterate on with natural language. No technical skills required to use it. You can watch a short demo (under a minute) at https://youtu.be/NbA28Pshxyo or click around some demo exports in your browser without installing anything: https://codeyam-ai.github.io/cadyam-exports/

We were also inspired by the HN threads about creative tools rebuilt in Rust, e.g. discussed in this HN thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49959605

Some technical details:

- CadYam is written in Rust and runs a local MCP server. Agents connect to it and use the same commands you do, so they can drive almost everything in the app. CadYam has instructions for connecting a range of agents.

- We built CadYam with CodeYam (codeyam.com), a product we developed for building software with AI. It lets us develop quickly while keeping the app well organized and well tested. We're shipping about two dozen fixes and features a day (more than 600 in the last month), so feature suggestions and bug reports are welcome and should get fixed quickly.

- The app is currently free for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It probably won't be free forever, but if we do charge, it will be a small amount. It's inexpensive for us to develop, and it doubles as a demo of what you can build with CodeYam.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: We replaced our time tracking SaaS with a Git repository
records.author: snikolaev
records.storyText:
TL;DR:

- Free and open source, no seat limits.

  - Some of its features require plans that cost a team of 10 around $1,000/year on Clockify or $2,000/year on Toggl Track.
- No backend. Your time entries live in your private GitHub repo.

- Track any URL.

- Works offline, syncs in the background and keeps changes in Git history.

- Team reports, CSV exports, historical hourly rates, multiple currencies and PDF invoices, all in the browser.

Hi HN. I'm Sergey, one of the developers behind Manticore Search.

We'd been using Clockify for years until they decided to limit their free plan to five users recently. We started looking around. Being an open-source company, we weren't particularly excited about paying another monthly fee per employee. But we didn't want to self-host a server and a database for what is essentially a stopwatch either.

Then we thought: we already use GitHub for most of our work (dev, PM, CRM, CMS). Why not use it for time tracking too?

So we built Clockoli. Our whole team (Manticore Search) switched to it about a month ago, and so far it's been working well for us.

Each team member writes to their own branch. Even if we abandon Clockoli tomorrow, your synced data isn't going anywhere. Just git clone the repo and do whatever you want with it: look through the history, write your own scripts, let an AI agent analyze the data or even build your own tools around it.

There are downsides, of course. You depend on GitHub. Anyone with read access to the repo can see the team's time entries, so if you need to keep some of them private from your teammates, this might not be for you. Hourly rates, though, are stored in your browser and never committed to the repo.

It works for us, but I'm wondering if it would work for other teams too. Would you use something like this? If not, what would stop you?

records.title: Show HN: Budget – an open-source private budgeting app for Mac and Windows
records.author: hendriknl
records.storyText:
Budget is a free, open-source app for Mac and Windows. With the simple mode, it gives you what you'd expect of a budgeting app: configure budgets and track expenses against those budgets. But, if you're a geek like me and are way too interested in your personal finance, the extended mode offers features like carrying leftover budgets to the next month, splitting expenses across multiple budgets and seeing how much you can freely spend the coming year, while taking into account any large future expenses (like a car insurance where the premium is paid on a yearly basis).

This app is the result of a hobby of mine to track my expenses. It started a few years ago in a spreadsheet, but that spreadsheet at some point took me minutes to edit on my MacBook with 8 gigs of RAM. I had the idea to turn it into an app before, but never had the time to do so.

I worked in the software industry until halfway through 2024, when LLMs were mostly just used for debugging. But, because of all the positivity I heard about how good they've gotten now, I tried to see if I could turn the spreadsheet into an app with the help of Claude Opus 5.5. I had to point out a couple of bugs and bad decisions (like bad alignment of text and using entire English sentences instead of keywords as keys for translation), but overall, it worked really well.

Budgeting apps are of course not new. But, they often are either free but with limited features, free but with an obnoxious amount of cookies and/or ads, free but charge money for important features or charge money to be used at all. The idea of this project is that there are no cookies, no ads, no fees, no data being stored remotely and that the code is open-source. Data ownership stands at the center of the app: you can easily export/import your data and create back-ups (besides the automatic back-ups the app creates for you). It is available to everyone, of course as long as you have a device that is supported (currently only devices that run macOS and Windows).

I'm interested to hear if you think this app has any potential and if you think any important features are missing.

records.title: Show HN: Brickie – deploy sandboxes in your own AWS account
records.author: abelanger
records.storyText:
Hey HN, this is Alexander from Hatchet (https://github.com/hatchet-dev/hatchet). We’re releasing a new open-source project today called Brickie. Brickie lets you run sandboxes in your own cloud account, primarily targeting EKS on AWS.

Sandboxes are an incredibly useful primitive for agentic applications. They serve two main functions: (1) a way for the agent to safely execute untrusted code, and (2) a durable filesystem for agents to preserve their state via snapshots.

We decided to start building this after we started on a package called `@hatchet-dev/sandbox` to integrate more directly with various sandbox providers, like E2B, Daytona, Archil, and Modal. We discovered that a lot of users had a requirement to self-host their sandbox infra for part of (or all of) their stack, due to a self-host requirement for enterprises. We searched around for the easiest way for users to self-host a sandbox stack and agent-sandbox (https://agent-sandbox.sigs.k8s.io) was the closest thing to what we had in mind: it’s a kubernetes-sigs project implementing a Kubernetes operator which spawns sandboxes as pods on supported isolation layers like Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata Containers. We learned that many platform teams were adopting this because it's a standard k8s-based deployment model and is pretty easy to customize the isolation layer, network config, etc.

However, it was missing some necessary features. brickie builds on top of the agent-sandbox project and extends it to support proper sandbox (filesystem-based) snapshots, fork, pause, and resume, all while bundling a proper orchestration and observability layer via Hatchet.

Zooming out a bit, Hatchet is an orchestration engine which supports durable execution (https://hatchet.run/blog/durable-execution). Throughout 2026, we saw high adoption from users building agents using durable workflows as the statefulness layer and execution model. But as sandboxes became more popular, something didn’t sit right with us. Sandboxes _also_ provide a durability layer, but at the filesystem level, and it became important to disambiguate what we call session state from filesystem state. I wrote a lot more about this here: https://hatchet.run/blog/agent-statefulness.

The problem with having state in multiple places is that it needs coordination, which adds complexity to your application. This was part of the motivation behind `@hatchet-dev/sandbox`: we wanted to provide an easy way to take coordinated snapshots of agent state, even when using an external sandbox provider.

So when we started looking at self-hosted sandbox options, it was critical that this architecture was supported well. We decided to support this in brickie using a pretty simple snapshotting mechanism which tars and stores snapshots in an object store (S3). This is something we’re actively working to improve and make more performant.

Brickie is early and in beta, we're looking for testers, contributors, and feedback on the deployment model. Thanks in advance!

RCHIVE is a cross-platform desktop app for cataloging, searching and reorganizing files on your computers and drives. Like, all of 'em: internal, external, network shares, USB sticks, loose SD cards, weird CD-R's, DVDs, floppy disks, Zip disks, and everything in between.

I built this thing because my digital archives are an embarrassment! 30 years of getting a new hard drive whenever capacity quadrupled and dragging the old one to it into a folder titled "BACKUP - TO SORT" will do that to you lol, especially when you know deep down that "sorting" will never happen. To try to deal with that growing mess on a daily basis, I've tried a patchwork of all of our favorites in the past -- Everything, grep, custom scripts, you name it. And don't get me started on built-in OS defaults like Windows Explorer, Finder, Spotlight. I figured it was time to make something better-suited to my tastes, and 4200 commits later here we are!

RCHIVE scans as many different sources as you throw at it, gives you unified deep search across the entire catalog (with drives connected or disconnected), allows you to virtually organize and clean up giant archives of digital stuff by applying recipes and transformations, resiliently copies or moves files when you're ready to actually restructure on disk, or just lets you quickly pop in to find something or browse everything with previews, metadata, etc.

It works on Windows, Mac or Linux, works offline, has zero telemetry, deletes nothing, and is fully deterministic in operation. So, no wacky AI integrations for decision making or classification, everything is predictable and repeatable, you can even run portable versions off of a USB drive if you don't want to install it.

I've been using it all day every day for a year and am just stoked to have it out there, get some users, get some feedback (good or bad), and see what people think. There's a free trial, no email address or anything needed.

The website is also full of videos, features, comparisons, all that stuff, as well as a ncdu-like companion app for figuring out where the hell all your disk space went.

Anyways, check it out! Should come in handy if you're ever in Grand Central trying to find a garbage file left on some dude's Gibson.

https://www.rchive.computer

Each agent gives its side, its evidence and a private mandate from its human, for example "may pay up to $300". The mediator never sees either mandate, so it proposes on the merits. records.title: Show HN: Modeloop – Design and simulate discrete-time controllers in the browser
records.author: lucamark
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I’d like to share a new model-based design environment with anyone interested in trying it out. It’s free and you can start modeling in the browser without installing any desktop software.

It's called Modeloop and we've spent some years to build but we think it has a lot of interesting features.

DIAGRAMS

In the diagram editor, you can build control algorithms by combining basic blocks from the standard library and use finite state machines (FSMs) to define operating modes and the transitions between them. You can organize your diagram into nested subsystems and schedule different functions to run at different rates. For example, you could run a motor’s current loop at 10 kHz, its speed loop at 1 kHz and its diagnostics at 100 Hz.

You can also edit any model either graphically or as text. For example:

previous = UnitDelay(filtered_value, initial=20.0)

new_sample = 0.2 * raw

memory = 0.8 * previous

filtered_value = new_sample + memory

filtered = filtered_value

The model format is open, and models are saved as JSON, without obscure proprietary formats that lead to vendor lock-in. There’s also a built-in version control system that lets you commit your diagrams and push them to GitHub, for example.

ENGINE

Modeloop’s engine is written in Rust to give users maximum performance while minimizing wait times, especially during compilation and simulation. You can also write unit tests for specific parts of the model, create different scenarios, and view test coverage for the automatically generated code.

Modeloop supports both Model-in-the-loop and Software-in-the-loop simulations. The broader documentation is at https://www.modeloop.app/docs.

We’d love to hear your feedback on the product, the parts you love and especially what’s unclear or could be improved.

Two years ago, I tried making a sudoku game in React, but I let it go because getting everything properly implemented turned out to be quite a bit of work. Then AI came along. I’ve spent the past few weeks working hard on Klink in the evenings and on weekends.

It started out with experimenting a Tamagotchi-style game where you had to take care of a little robot and gradually add more parts to it. But it turned out that a Tamagotchi on an iPhone didn’t really work, I was just mashing buttons and it didn't give me that same feeling I got as a kid clicking the little buttons to feed my pixelated friend. I then thought of a talk given by Theo (the T3 Youtuber) about how we should all think bigger when working with AI and I’ve always wanted to make a sudoku game. So that got me thinking about the sudoku games/apps I played in the past.

I’ve always found sudoku games a bit dry. Other than a "Daily Challenge" there isn't really an incentive to have me coming back and then after a few days I forget all about it. So I started with prompting and kept prompting and prompting until I’d built a sudoku app that was actually usable, with one extra mechanic: building and upgrading a little robot. The flow of the game is that you solve a puzzle, this gives you scrap, that scrap is then used to "buy" new components, or upgrade existing components. (each component has Mk I, Mk II, Mk III versions)

I'm Dutch and it's Sinterklaas season here, so I added an in-game event where you can earn robot parts themed around the holiday. They're only available during this time of the year. Up next will probably be Christmas.

Alongside classic sudoku, I added quite a few variants (Killer, Thermo, Sandwich, Arrows, Diagonal, Chaos (Jigsaw), Kropki, Even/Odd, Hyper, Binaro, and Trees and Tents). I also added “Tricks,” which are basically short lessons on how to use standard sudoku techniques and recognize patterns. Then I polished the app a bit more and finally released it to the App Store last Friday. You can play it on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Since Friday, I’ve had a whopping 15 downloads, mostly from friends and family (to be honest, probably all of them). I also made a website: https://klinksudoku.com. Normally I just work as a developer at a company and this is my first time I actually have to think about things like marketing, getting more users, promoting the product which is very fun to experience.

Currently I’m also looking for Android testers. Since I have a personal developer account, Google requires me to have 12 people in a closed test before I can release the app publicly. You can join the test group here: https://groups.google.com/g/klink-sudoku-testers

records.title: Show HN: Ribbon Architect – Endless ways to tie a gift ribbon
records.author: permute
records.storyText:
Ribbon Architect is available as a free iOS app and in the browser.

Scan or measure a gift, browse pattern suggestions made for its exact proportions, or construct your own designs. Then step-by-step instructions show you how to lay the ribbon on your gift.

Gifts are modeled as convex polyhedra, so many non-cuboid gift shapes, such as prisms, work too and have their own interesting ribbon patterns.

A ribbon (without twists) that is pulled tight follows a locally shortest path, a geodesic. This is a path on the surface of the gift that runs straight on faces and folds correctly over edges and loops back on itself. As you'll see in the app, geodesics can be much more interesting than the axis-aligned loops that people usually tie when wrapping a gift.

Click "Browse geodesics" on the first screen of the app, to get a glimpse of the endless variety of geodesics. (It currently stops after 5'000 or earlier depending on available memory. In theory, a box has infinitely many distinct geodesics.)

For further variety, you can combine these building blocks by inserting twists: When twisted, two strands of ribbon that follow sections of geodesics that cross, turn over and follow the other geodesic. This can join two geodesics into a single ribbon. Click any crossing to insert a twist (after selecting a pattern or after drawing ribbons in "draw your own" mode). Or follow the tutorial (the ? icon in the upper right corner).

This is the first version. The browser version hasn't been tested on many browsers and devices. Please let me know if you run into any issues.

records.title: Show HN: Pi-maestro – spec driven development for Pi
records.author: emiliospme
records.storyText:
https://github.com/emilioSp/pi-maestro

Pi Maestro started from my need to use an engineering method when working with agents. With simple prompts or the "let’s write a plan" approach, I would sometimes reach dead ends and have to start over. Agents would say the work was complete too early, without checking the result enough.

Spec-driven development seemed suitable for this problem.

So I tried to turn it into a workflow that worked in practice: define the expected behavior, ask one agent to implement it, and ask another to check it independently.

At first, I tried to do everything through skills. However, I noticed that agents would skip steps in the protocol described in the Markdown files. My impression was that following the workflow required too much attention compared to the assigned task.

So I introduced deterministic tools that control transitions and check the reports produced by agents. Basically, I built a finite state machine where each step requires a structured handoff. This handoff also becomes the starting point for the next agent.

Taking inspiration from OpenSpec and GitHub Spec Kit, I adopted the concepts that suited the way I work:

proposal.md for the context, goal, and scope of the change.

spec.md for requirements in the form "actor MUST…" and acceptance criteria using GIVEN, WHEN, THEN and concrete examples.

design.md when important technical decisions are needed.

Once the spec is written and approved, the Maestro (orchestrator) starts coordinating a sequence of agents:

Builder, responsible for implementation.

Verifier, responsible for checking that everything works as specified.

Simplifier, responsible for simplifying the code to make it clearer.

I have chosen Pi because it provides events to control the runtime. This made it easy to add the maestro without going through an MCP server.

Pi also works with different LLM models. Using different models for each role allows for a more critical view of the spec: a builder and a verifier from the same "family" will approach the problem in similar ways.

I'd like to have your feedback on it and in general on the spec-driven development.

Do you use spec-driven development? If Yes, which workflow best suit for your needs?

records.title: Show HN: Outloud Reader – photograph a page and listen to it phrase by phrase
records.author: storogenko
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I built Outloud Reader, an iOS and Android app that reads any page aloud. You take a photo of a page, open a PDF, or paste text, and it reads it aloud in a natural voice, highlighting each phrase as it is spoken.

How the idea was born:

My wife has been learning English for many years but she never gets real practice. One day she told me it would be great to have an app that could turn any photo of text into audio, so she could practice her listening while walking or driving. That's what inspired me to build Outloud Reader.

Yes, I know there are many text-to-speech apps, but most of them just read the text or cost too much.

What it does:

- Every phrase lights up as it's spoken, so you can read along

- 14 languages, with a woman's or a man's voice in most of them

- If you're learning a language, it can translate the page into the language you're learning

- If you have nothing to listen to, ask AI to write a short text at your level (A1–C2) and turn it into audio

- The finished audio is stored on your phone, so it works offline

- On iPhone and iPad your library syncs through iCloud, so you can start on your phone and keep listening on your tablet

- No sign-up, no email, no ads

How it works:

The page goes to my server, an LLM recognizes the text and translates it if you ask, then it is voiced with a mix of open-source and cloud voices depending on the language. The phrase highlighting comes from aligning the audio with the text. The apps are native on both platforms.

The app is free to download and gives you a few free pages to try it. After that you need a subscription or pre-paid pages that never expire. All the audio you've created stays yours to listen to as much as you like, no subscription needed.

Plans: I'm working on a web + API version and already have a small waiting list.

What would you listen to first: textbooks, articles, or books in another language? I'll be here all day. Any feedback, bugs or ideas are very welcome!

I run a small school for gifted kids in Honolulu, and our students do some of their math practice on iPads. I wanted a 9-year-old to be able to type 3 2/5 the way she'd write it on paper, and couldn't find a React Native component that did it. MathLive and MathQuill are good editors, but they're built on the DOM, so in React Native they only run inside a WebView, and I didn't want a WebView inside every answer box.

It's harder than you might think to to make sure arrow keys, taps in parentheses, delete keys, tab key, etc. on a hardware keyboard all work as expected. We packaged it up so other schools/builders don't need to reinvent the wheel.

It's drawn with react-native-svg and runs in Expo Go. A dev build adds two small iOS modules.

We pulled it out of the tutoring app our students use every day and put it under MIT. It hasn't been run on Android yet. Web support is new in 0.1.1: 0.1.0 crashed on react-native-web, which I found out while taking a screenshot for this post.

records.title: Show HN: CertNudge – Cert and domain expiry alerts
records.author: HallowDance
records.storyText:
As you probably know, Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry reminder emails in June 2025. Furthermore, certificate lifetimes are shrinking: 200 days since March 2026, 100 days from March 2027, 47(!) days by 2029. Automation is supposed to handle that, and it does most of the time, but it can fail. More often than not, you find out about a missed renewal when your users report a big warning in their browser tabs. This might lead to frustration, angry emails, and rushing to find out the extent of the affected domains.

I built CertNudge, a small tool that checks what each host actually serves. Every six hours it connects with SNI and verifies the chain to check that SSL certificates are valid and not about to expire. Additionally it checks the domain registration expiry over RDAP once a day. For failed checks and upcoming expiry it alerts you by email (or Slack/Discord/Telegram on Pro) 30, 14, 7, 3, 1 and 0 days before expiry.

I've deliberately decided to keep the stack as low to the ground as possible: Flask, SQLite, server-rendered pages that work fully without JavaScript (although there are some JS goodies and animations that are non-essential). Payments go through Stripe over plain HTTPS without the SDK. Account management is simple as possible, login goes through an email link, no passwords are generated or stored.

The service is free for up to 3 hosts. If you want more, the Pro tier is 5 €/month or 50 €/year for up to 100 hosts plus Slack/Discord webhooks and Telegram alerts. There's also a one-off checker and a bulk checker you can use without an account.

Hopefully this proves useful for somebody! I'll be happy to discuss possible extensions and welcome all critique.

records.title: Show HN: 11 Three.js towns to practise 9 languages, live voice and open chat

records.storyText:
As somebody that is not a natural learning languages, I found it really hard to get enough practise to feel confident speaking when you actually have someone to talk to someone. I wanted somewhere to practise everyday conversation out lout, so I made Maido.

It's a free game in your browser and works on desktop or mobile with nothing to install and no login or account needed. You can even sync progress between your devices via an encrypted blind relay by using a QR code.

Each language has a 3D town where you walk around, talk to people with your mic (or by typing) and run ordinary errands like ordering food, buying flowers, getting groceries, and talking with neighbours. Each place has a number of districts you can travel around and a story unfolds as you go along. The characters answer in their own language with life like voices, with translations and explanations tailored to the skill level you are on.

Open-ended conversations use hosted AI (I'm paying for this out of pocket). There is a 10 minute allowance per day to keep it manageable. Once that runs out, the scripted engine kicks in, or you can BYOK with your own (free) Gemini API key. This also unlocks Gemini Live mode where the response is nearly instant. There are no ads or payments at the moment.

For the TLDR crowd, I've been learning Japanese for a very long time so Yunagi is the flagship town. You can jump to it directly here - https://maido.place/yunagi/

I'll make a longer post below on how it's built and more technical bits. Would love any feedback, bug reports, etc. on https://github.com/nyblnet/maido-community or hello@maido.place
